title: POC scoping: EU-only Hosted API (region pinning + enforcement)
summary: Nordholm Payments scoped a 2–3 week POC for EU-only processing on Redwood Hosted API. Customer success criteria focus on deterministic region pinning (no cross-region fallback), clear residency violation errors, and latency/throughput targets for chat + structured outputs. Redwood walked through the planned enforcement behavior (allowed region set + primary region, request-time checks, blocking behavior, and audit/observability signals) and agreed on a concrete test matrix (EU pinned key hitting US base URL, streaming/non-streaming parity, model fallback disabled by default). Next steps include sending a POC plan, pinning configuration instructions, and confirming exact regions and metrics definitions.
topics: POC goals and success criteria (EU-only hosted inference)
Region pinning policy model (org/project/api key) and precedence
Enforcement behavior: routing, fallback, background jobs, logs/traces
Error contract for residency blocks (status, code, request_id, help URL)
Rollout / allowlist and how to validate in staging vs prod
next_steps: Redwood (Hannah/Markus) to send a 1-pager POC plan with success criteria, test cases, and timelines.
Redwood to confirm EU region options for Hosted (primary + allowed set) and the recommended configuration for Nordholm.
Customer (Marek) to share representative request distribution (prompt lengths, max_tokens, concurrency) and the exact endpoints they will call.
Customer (Ines) to send their required wording for 'data residency' and any audit log expectations for the POC security packet.
Schedule a technical validation session to run the region-pinning negative tests (EU pinned key -> US endpoint) and capture screenshots/log evidence.
action_items: Owner: Hannah Schmitt — Send POC scoping email + calendar for technical validation session — Due: 2025-02-19
Owner: Markus Klein — Share sample curl + SDK snippets for setting region pinning and reproducing a residency block (streaming + non-streaming) — Due: 2025-02-20
Owner: Naomi Feldman — Provide latest public-facing explanation of what is/isn't covered by Hosted residency (logs/traces, fallback) for Nordholm security review — Due: 2025-02-20
Owner: Marek Kowalski — Provide workload stats (P50/P95 input tokens, output tokens, concurrency) and the model short-list — Due: 2025-02-21
Owner: Ines Bauer — Provide required compliance checks list (SOC2/ISO, subprocessors, audit log fields) for POC gating — Due: 2025-02-21
questions: Can we hard-block any cross-region failover even during incidents? (Answer: yes, default behavior is block; customer can explicitly allow additional EU regions as allowed set.)
How do you handle streaming errors—do we get a generic 500 or a deterministic residency error? (Answer: plan is consistent error contract; streaming returns structured error + request_id.)
Do logs or traces ever contain prompt content outside the pinned region? (Answer: content is treated as in-scope; logging is region-bounded; metadata may be centralized depending on configuration.)
What exact latency metric do we use—time-to-first-token vs full completion? (Answer: both; TTFT for UX and end-to-end for cost/throughput.)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-02-18
Start time: 15:05 UTC
Duration: 52 min
Title: POC scoping: EU-only Hosted API (region pinning + enforcement)
Attendees:
- Hannah Schmitt (Redwood, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood, Product - Security & Compliance)
- Lars Nordholm (Nordholm Payments, VP Eng)
- Ines Bauer (Nordholm, Security/Compliance)
- Marek Kowalski (Nordholm, Platform)

Auto-summary (generated by Fireflies)
- Discussed EU-only region pinning, request-time enforcement, and error handling.
- Agreed on success metrics for latency and residency compliance evidence.
- Next steps: Redwood to send POC plan, docs, and schedule validation tests.

Transcript
[00:00] Hannah Schmitt: Cool, thanks everyone for joining. Uh, this is Hannah from Redwood. Markus is here as well, and Naomi from our security and compliance product side.
[00:10] Hannah Schmitt: The goal today is to scope the POC for an EU-only Hosted API deployment. So, what you want to test, what “success” means, and then also what the pinning enforcement will do and not do.
[00:23] Lars Nordholm: Yep. Thanks Hannah. For us the big thing is we can’t have prompts or outputs leaving the EU, even like during failover. We got burned once with a vendor where it quietly went to US West.
[00:35] Ines Bauer: And we need to be able to demonstrate it. Like, not just “trust me.” We need logs or some evidence for internal audit.
[00:44] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Maybe I’ll start with a quick framing and then we go into your workload and targets.
[00:50] Marek Kowalski: Sounds good.

[01:02] Markus Klein: So, on Hosted, we’re introducing region pinning as a policy you can set at org or project, and optionally override at the API key level.
[01:12] Markus Klein: The policy has an allowed region set, like “EU-only,” and a primary region. Routing checks that at request time. If the request would land outside the allowed set, we block.
[01:26] Lars Nordholm: Block as in… error back to us? Not like “it’ll try anyway.”
[01:29] Markus Klein: Correct. Deterministic block. No cross-region fallback unless you explicitly allow additional regions in the allowed set.
[01:37] Naomi Feldman: And from the product perspective, the default posture is conservative—no silent failover across boundaries.

[01:46] Hannah Schmitt: Before we get too deep, can we confirm the POC timeline? You mentioned 2–3 weeks last email.
[01:52] Lars Nordholm: Yeah. We want something we can run quickly. We’ve got procurement watching, but we can do a technical POC under a pilot agreement.
[01:59] Ines Bauer: The gating items are: EU-only enforcement, a clear statement of what data is stored where, and audit logs for config changes.

[02:12] Hannah Schmitt: Great. Marek, can you describe the workload? Like what endpoints, what token lengths, concurrency.
[02:19] Marek Kowalski: Sure. Two main things: chat completion for customer support summarization, and structured output for transaction categorization.
[02:28] Marek Kowalski: Prompts are, uh, average maybe 1.5k tokens input, but sometimes 6k. Output is like 200 to 800 tokens.
[02:36] Marek Kowalski: Concurrency: in peak, around 40 concurrent requests. Overall RPS maybe 10 to 20, but bursts.
[02:44] Markus Klein: Ok. And you’re streaming tokens to the UI or you wait for full completion?
[02:49] Marek Kowalski: For support UI we stream. For categorization we don’t.

[03:00] Hannah Schmitt: Latency targets—what are you holding vendors to?
[03:04] Lars Nordholm: For streaming, time to first token is the user-perceived one. We’d love under 300 milliseconds P95, but we know it depends.
[03:12] Lars Nordholm: End-to-end P95 under, say, two seconds for typical prompts.
[03:18] Marek Kowalski: Yeah and not too spiky. We see huge variance with Azure OpenAI in Europe sometimes.
[03:25] Hannah Schmitt: Got it. Markus can talk realistic targets by model class.

[03:31] Markus Klein: Sure. For Hosted EU regions, for a 70B-class model, TTFT P95 sub-300ms is ambitious depending on prompt length.
[03:40] Markus Klein: But we can target TTFT P95 ~350–500ms for your typical case, and completion latency depends on output tokens and sampling.
[03:49] Markus Klein: If you’re ok with a smaller model for categorization, we can get TTFT tighter.
[03:55] Marek Kowalski: We can evaluate. We’re open to a model trade. We mostly care about consistent formatting.

[04:06] Ines Bauer: I want to come back to enforcement boundaries. When you say “no prompts leave EU,” does that include logs? Like request logs, traces.
[04:14] Naomi Feldman: The intent is yes: “customer content” includes prompts and outputs and any derived embeddings that could reconstruct content.
[04:23] Naomi Feldman: For in-scope systems in the first release: routing decisions, gateway handling, and operational logs/traces that might capture content are constrained by region.
[04:34] Ines Bauer: “Might capture content” is the key. Because I’ve seen debug logs.
[04:39] Markus Klein: Totally fair. Practically, we recommend running with content logging off; but enforcement is designed so even if you had an error, the request body shouldn’t be shipped to a US log pipeline.
[04:52] Marek Kowalski: And what about metrics? Like aggregated counts.
[04:55] Naomi Feldman: Aggregated metadata like counts and latency histograms can be centralized, depending, but we can keep them EU-scoped for the POC if that’s required. The hard line is raw content.

[05:09] Lars Nordholm: Ok. But we need crisp language. Like, “This is in region, this is global.”
[05:15] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We’ll share the FAQ language and you can mark what’s mandatory for you.

[05:23] Hannah Schmitt: On pinning mechanics, are you expecting “EU-only” as a simple toggle in the console, or are you fine with an API setting for the POC?
[05:31] Marek Kowalski: For POC API is fine. Long term we want console + Terraform.
[05:35] Markus Klein: Ok. For the POC, we can set at project and issue you an API key that’s pinned. Then we can test.

[05:44] Marek Kowalski: Testing meaning, what? Like we call a US endpoint and it fails?
[05:49] Markus Klein: Exactly. There are a couple negative tests:
[05:52] Markus Klein: 1) EU-pinned key tries to route to a non-allowed region -> blocked.
[05:57] Markus Klein: 2) Capacity pressure triggers fallback attempt -> blocked if fallback would cross region.
[06:03] Markus Klein: 3) Streaming path returns same structured error as non-streaming.
[06:08] Ines Bauer: What’s the error? Like status code and body.

[06:13] Markus Klein: The proposed contract is HTTP 409 for residency policy violation.
[06:18] Markus Klein: Body includes a machine-readable error code, message, request_id, and a help URL.
[06:24] Markus Klein: The message would say something like “Request blocked by data residency policy: allowed regions [EU], attempted region [US]. Update your project residency settings or use an EU endpoint.”
[06:35] Marek Kowalski: 409 is interesting. Why not 403.
[06:38] Naomi Feldman: The thinking is it’s a conflict with configured policy. But the important part is it’s consistent and easy to catch.
[06:45] Hannah Schmitt: And the SDK will surface it as a dedicated exception type rather than a generic “server error.”

[06:54] Ines Bauer: For streaming, we’ve had cases where it starts streaming and then errors mid-way and we get a weird partial response.
[07:01] Markus Klein: Right. For residency blocks, it should be pre-flight. The gateway evaluates before any model execution, so you should get the error before tokens stream.
[07:11] Marek Kowalski: Unless there’s a redirect?
[07:13] Markus Klein: There is no redirect. It’s a direct block.

[07:20] Lars Nordholm: What regions are you offering in the EU?
[07:23] Hannah Schmitt: Today for Hosted we can do EU West (Ireland) and EU Central (Frankfurt). Exact naming depends on our internal region IDs, but those are the physical locations.
[07:34] Lars Nordholm: We’d prefer Frankfurt for latency to DACH.
[07:38] Markus Klein: Ok, so primary EU Central, allowed set could be just EU Central, or EU Central + EU West if you want intra-EU resilience.
[07:48] Ines Bauer: Is intra-EU failover acceptable from the product’s perspective?
[07:52] Lars Nordholm: Yes. We’re fine with EU-to-EU. We’re not fine with EU-to-US.

[08:01] Hannah Schmitt: Great. That’s a common setup: allowed = {EU-Central, EU-West}, primary = EU-Central.
[08:09] Marek Kowalski: But in an incident, would you auto-failover to EU West without telling us?
[08:14] Markus Klein: If it’s in the allowed set, yes, routing can choose it if policy allows and if primary is unhealthy.
[08:21] Markus Klein: But we can also configure it to “hard pin” to primary only for the POC, so you can see the block behavior.
[08:29] Lars Nordholm: That would be good to test both.

[08:33] Hannah Schmitt: Let’s outline POC success criteria. I’ll propose three buckets: residency, performance, and integration.
[08:41] Hannah Schmitt: Residency: 100% of requests served in allowed EU regions; any disallowed attempt returns deterministic error with request_id; and audit events for config changes.
[08:52] Ines Bauer: Add: no content in logs outside EU. Even if you store metrics elsewhere, we need confirmation content is not leaving.
[09:00] Naomi Feldman: Ok, we’ll capture that.

[09:04] Hannah Schmitt: Performance: hit TTFT P95 target for representative prompts, and stable error rate.
[09:10] Marek Kowalski: Let’s define TTFT and end-to-end precisely. TTFT measured at our client.
[09:16] Markus Klein: That’s fine. We can also provide server-side timing headers.
[09:21] Marek Kowalski: Like x-request-id and timing.
[09:24] Markus Klein: Yes, request_id and a couple timing metrics.

[09:31] Hannah Schmitt: Integration: use our endpoint in your staging environment, run with your prompt set, and validate structured output reliability.
[09:38] Lars Nordholm: Yep.

[09:44] Ines Bauer: What about data retention? Are you storing prompts.
[09:48] Naomi Feldman: For Hosted, by default we do not persist prompt content for training. Operational retention depends on logging settings; the default is minimal, and we can set stricter retention for enterprise.
[10:03] Ines Bauer: Ok, but I need specifics. Like “0 days” or “X days.”
[10:09] Hannah Schmitt: We’ll send the security packet with the defaults and options.

[10:18] Marek Kowalski: Current stack wise, we have a gateway in front, we sign requests, and we call either OpenAI or Azure OpenAI. For EU we currently call West Europe.
[10:28] Marek Kowalski: We need to be sure there’s no DNS trick where it resolves to somewhere else.
[10:34] Markus Klein: Understood. We can provide region-specific base URLs. And in addition, region pinning will check even if you hit the “wrong” URL.
[10:44] Marek Kowalski: Wait, so if I call a US base URL with an EU pinned key it blocks.
[10:49] Markus Klein: Exactly.
[10:51] Marek Kowalski: Good.

[11:00] Lars Nordholm: How is this different from dedicated? Our CTO asked if we should just do Dedicated in Frankfurt.
[11:07] Hannah Schmitt: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and isolation, and we can do residency constraints there too. For this POC, Hosted is fastest, and we can validate the policy model.
[11:18] Markus Klein: Also your throughput is modest; Hosted should be fine for a first pass.

[11:26] Ines Bauer: Who can change the policy? We need RBAC.
[11:29] Naomi Feldman: Policy changes are admin-scoped in the console; for API it’s restricted to admin tokens. Each change emits an audit log event.
[11:39] Ines Bauer: Audit log includes who, what, when.
[11:41] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Actor, timestamp, old/new config, and the object ID.
[11:48] Lars Nordholm: Do you expose the policy ID in the block error.
[11:52] Markus Klein: It may include a policy_id for supportability; if that’s a concern we can discuss. You’ll always get request_id.
[12:01] Ines Bauer: It’s okay as long as it’s not sensitive.

[12:08] Hannah Schmitt: Let’s talk model selection quickly. Are you evaluating a specific open model?
[12:14] Marek Kowalski: We were looking at Llama 3 70B and also smaller like 8B for categorization.
[12:19] Markus Klein: Great. We can set you up with two models and compare cost/latency.
[12:25] Marek Kowalski: We care about deterministic JSON. Does tool calling work?
[12:30] Markus Klein: Yes, we support structured outputs and function/tool calling patterns. We can share a template.

[12:38] Lars Nordholm: On cost, not a huge part of POC but we need ballpark.
[12:42] Hannah Schmitt: We’ll include pricing ranges in the follow-up, but for POC we’ll put you on credits.

[12:50] Ines Bauer: On incident behavior: if the EU region is down and we’ve allowed only EU Central, you will block rather than reroute to US.
[12:59] Markus Klein: Correct. You will see blocks. That’s the tradeoff.
[13:03] Lars Nordholm: That’s fine, we prefer fail closed.

[13:08] Hannah Schmitt: Ok. Evidence requirements: what exactly do you need to show internal audit.
[13:13] Ines Bauer: Three things: (1) written statement, (2) audit events for config changes, (3) proof that a request is blocked when it would go outside EU.
[13:24] Ines Bauer: Screenshots plus logs with request_id is fine.
[13:27] Naomi Feldman: We can do that. We’ll provide a small evidence pack for the POC.

[13:36] Marek Kowalski: How do we validate “no content leaves EU” though.
[13:40] Markus Klein: For the POC, we can show you the residency decision log fields: policy evaluated, selected region, and the reason. Those are generated in-region.
[13:50] Markus Klein: Separately, we can show that requests with a canary string never appear in non-EU log stores. But that’s more internal.
[13:59] Ines Bauer: Even a statement from your side is ok for POC, but for production we’ll need more.
[14:04] Hannah Schmitt: Understood.

[14:10] (crosstalk)
[14:10] Lars Nordholm: Sorry—just to clarify. If we allow EU West as backup, do you guarantee it won’t hit US even if both EU regions are down.
[14:19] Markus Klein: Yes. If allowed set is EU-only, then it won’t route to US. If nothing in allowed set is healthy, it blocks.

[14:31] Hannah Schmitt: Ok. Let’s map out the POC steps.
[14:35] Hannah Schmitt: Step 1: Redwood provisions a project, sets residency policy: primary EU Central; allowed EU Central only for the strict test.
[14:45] Hannah Schmitt: Step 2: you run integration with your staging gateway.
[14:50] Hannah Schmitt: Step 3: negative test: call US endpoint with EU key; verify 409 + error_code + request_id.
[14:58] Hannah Schmitt: Step 4: enable allowed EU West; simulate EU Central degraded; verify routing stays in EU.
[15:06] Marek Kowalski: Simulate how. Can you force it.
[15:09] Markus Klein: We can use a test header in staging or we can temporarily disable a region for your project during a scheduled window.
[15:18] Marek Kowalski: Ok.

[15:22] Hannah Schmitt: Do you need SSO or SAML for POC.
[15:25] Lars Nordholm: Not for POC.
[15:27] Ines Bauer: For production yes, but not gating.

[15:32] Marek Kowalski: One thing: we had a vendor where streaming errors came as generic 500. We need it consistent.
[15:38] Markus Klein: Agreed. The goal is consistent error payload across streaming and non-streaming.
[15:44] Naomi Feldman: It’s explicitly part of the enterprise foundation work.

[15:51] Hannah Schmitt: Any other stakeholders we need to pull in.
[15:54] Lars Nordholm: Procurement will ask later. For now it’s us.

[16:02] Ines Bauer: Subprocessors: are you using any US-based logging vendor.
[16:07] Naomi Feldman: We do have subprocessors, but for residency we scope where customer content goes. We’ll share the subprocessor list and region info.
[16:17] Ines Bauer: Ok.

[16:21] Marek Kowalski: For our measurement, we’ll run a load test from Frankfurt. We can also run from Ireland.
[16:27] Markus Klein: That’s good. We’ll want to capture client-side TTFT and server timings. Also ensure you set max_tokens to representative values.

[16:39] Hannah Schmitt: Any constraints around KMS or customer-managed keys.
[16:43] Ines Bauer: Not for POC.

[16:47] Lars Nordholm: Let’s talk about “EU-only Hosted” wording. We want “processing and storage in EU.”
[16:54] Naomi Feldman: For Hosted, “processing in EU” is strong. “Storage” depends on what you mean by storage. We don’t store prompts as application data by default, but some operational artifacts exist.
[17:06] Naomi Feldman: We’ll provide language that’s accurate: request processing and content-bearing logs remain in the pinned region; configuration and account metadata may be global unless you choose the enterprise option.
[17:19] Ines Bauer: We need to review that.

[17:23] Hannah Schmitt: Ok. We’ll send the draft and you can mark required. For the POC, we can keep it simple: no prompt logging, strict pinning.

[17:33] Marek Kowalski: How do we disable prompt logging.
[17:36] Markus Klein: It’s a project setting; we can set it for you. And the SDK can be configured to not send extra debug fields.
[17:44] Marek Kowalski: Ok.

[17:49] (small pause)
[17:50] Hannah Schmitt: Anything else on latency. You said TTFT P95 300ms ideal. If we can’t hit that for 6k prompts, what’s acceptable.
[17:58] Lars Nordholm: For long prompts, it can be higher. The UI uses shorter ones typically.
[18:04] Marek Kowalski: Define two buckets: <=2k tokens and >2k tokens.
[18:08] Markus Klein: Great. We can report separate distributions.

[18:15] Hannah Schmitt: Perfect. We’ll capture that in the POC plan.

[18:20] Naomi Feldman: One more: are you expecting the residency block to be distinguishable from a general capacity issue.
[18:26] Ines Bauer: Yes.
[18:27] Naomi Feldman: Ok. The error_code will be specific to residency policy, not generic “unavailable.”

[18:34] Marek Kowalski: Do you have an example error_code.
[18:37] Markus Klein: Something like RESIDENCY_POLICY_VIOLATION or REGION_PINNING_VIOLATION. Exact string to confirm.
[18:45] Hannah Schmitt: We’ll send the current contract draft.

[18:51] Lars Nordholm: Great.

[19:00] (conversation continues with detailed planning; some repetitions omitted by transcription engine)

[23:12] Marek Kowalski: Sorry, I lost you—did you say 401 or 409.
[23:15] Markus Klein: 409.
[23:16] Marek Kowalski: Ok.

[28:41] Ines Bauer: If the request is blocked, do you still write anything to logs.
[28:46] Markus Klein: Minimal. Decision context, no prompt body. We can configure it to be extremely sparse.
[28:55] Naomi Feldman: And you still get request_id and an audit trail of the decision.

[34:10] Hannah Schmitt: Let’s lock timeline. If we send the POC plan tomorrow, can you start integration this week.
[34:16] Marek Kowalski: Yes, Friday.
[34:18] Lars Nordholm: Assuming we get keys and endpoint.
[34:21] Markus Klein: We can provision same day.

[41:02] Hannah Schmitt: Ok, last check—primary region preference Frankfurt, allowed set initially only Frankfurt, then optionally add Ireland for resilience testing.
[41:10] Lars Nordholm: Correct.

[46:25] Hannah Schmitt: Recap and next steps.
[46:27] Hannah Schmitt: Redwood will send: POC plan, pinning config instructions, draft residency language, and error contract examples.
[46:36] Hannah Schmitt: Nordholm will send: workload stats, prompt set sample, and your internal compliance checklist.
[46:44] Hannah Schmitt: Then we schedule a technical validation session early next week to run the negative tests and capture evidence.
[46:52] Lars Nordholm: Good.
[46:53] Ines Bauer: Works.
[46:55] Marek Kowalski: Yep.

[47:02] Hannah Schmitt: Anything else before we drop.
[47:05] Ines Bauer: No.
[47:06] Lars Nordholm: Thanks.
[47:07] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript
